title: Chip Security Moves From Checkbox Compliance To Continuous Defense
gist: A closed-door DAC roundtable of security execs from Arteris, Cadence, Keysight, Rambus, Siemens EDA, Synaptics, and Synopsys concludes that certification (CRA, ISO 26262, CSIP Level 3) is being treated as a check-box AAA-rating exercise that doesn't guarantee real security, chiplet supply chains and software/FPGA attack surfaces have outrun verification, and the EU Cyber Resilience Act's September 11, 2026 deadline plus a still-unenforced 4%-of-revenue penalty is the main forcing function pushing real investment — alongside a slow, patchwork transition to post-quantum crypto bottlenecked by legacy Public Key Accelerator (PKA) hardware.

insights.claim: Rambus' Scott Best says many customers treat security IP purchases (side-channel protection, fault-injection defense, PUF technology) as a check-box exercise to claim CRA or ISO 26262 adherence and CSIP Level 3 certification, without regard to whether the feature is actually deployed correctly in the system.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Certification-driven demand can inflate security IP revenue (Rambus, Synopsys, Arteris) without corresponding improvement in actual product security — investors should distinguish IP bookings growth from real risk reduction when evaluating this end market.
insights.quote: I require side-channel protection, I require fault injection attack, I need PUF technology
insights.locator: Best: There’s an important part about personal accountability

insights.claim: Rambus' Scott Best compares security certification to the AAA credit ratings dramatized in The Big Short: rating agencies stamped AAA on products they knew were flawed because 'customers wouldn't buy it' otherwise, and he sees the same dynamic in chip security certification today.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Signals systemic incentive misalignment in the security-certification market: certifiers and vendors are compensated for passing the audit, not for reducing breach risk, a structural red flag for anyone underwriting 'certified secure' as a moat.
insights.quote: How could you possibly put a AAA rating on this stuff that you knew was garbage?
insights.locator: Best: There’s an important part about personal accountability

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel states plainly that current certification is 'just enough to make the claim' needed to sell into the market, not proof of actual security.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Reinforces that compliance labels are a sales/marketing checkbox rather than a security guarantee — buyers of 'certified' chips (OEMs, integrators) still bear residual security risk despite paperwork.
insights.quote: That’s just enough to make the claim to get that AAA rating so that you can sell it into the market.
insights.locator: Hinkel: That’s just enough to make the claim

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Chris Giles argues awareness of security's importance is now widespread across the industry, but actual investment reflects internal prioritization, not stated belief — and incentives, not education, are what change priority.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: For investors assessing which chip/EDA vendors will actually harden products, watch for regulatory or contractual incentives (fines, procurement requirements) rather than vendor messaging about 'caring about security.'
insights.locator: Giles: From what I see, I completely agree

insights.claim: Cadence's Yathiendra Vunnam says customers are increasingly building security via chiplets and open frameworks like OCP Caliptra — plugging in a security subsystem on a specific chiplet fabricated at a cheaper node rather than using the most advanced node for every block, to cut device cost.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Chiplet-based security subsystems could become a distinct, higher-margin IP category (mixed-node security chiplets) separate from the compute die — worth tracking OCP Caliptra ecosystem adoption as a proxy for chiplet security standardization.
insights.locator: Vunnam: We’ve been seeing a lot of defense-in-depth

insights.claim: Cadence's Yathiendra Vunnam identifies verifying which chiplet in a multi-source, multi-vendor assembly is actually secure as 'probably the biggest hurdle right now' for customers building chiplet-based systems.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Unsolved cross-chiplet security verification is a gating risk for the broader chiplet/UCIe ecosystem's adoption in security-sensitive markets (defense, automotive, finance) — a potential wedge for EDA/verification vendors building chiplet trust-verification tools.
insights.quote: How do you verify which chiplet is secure and which isn’t?
insights.locator: Vunnam: ...That’s probably the biggest hurdle right now

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr describes modern data centers as hierarchically assembled from IC to package to board to system to network into 'town-sized systems that are fully connected everywhere,' making the network itself one of the primary attack bottlenecks.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: As system complexity compounds across hierarchy levels, attack surface grows faster than any single layer's defenses — reinforces demand for network-level (not just chip-level) security monitoring in hyperscale AI datacenters.
insights.quote: you’re basically building town-sized systems that are fully connected everywhere
insights.locator: Petr: The distinction we need to make here is

themes.theme: Software, firmware, and AI-driven attack surface

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr says the software bill of materials (SBOM) for hardware is becoming critical because attacks — especially AI-driven attacks — increasingly enter through the network and trigger vulnerabilities in embedded software and FPGA firmware rather than through direct physical attacks on silicon.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: SBOM-for-hardware is emerging as a compliance and product requirement analogous to software SBOMs post-SolarWinds — a growth category for security tooling vendors (Keysight EDA, Synopsys, Cadence) selling component-visibility platforms.
insights.locator: Petr: The complexity we see is that software

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr warns that open-source components used deep in embedded and FPGA software stacks are a growing threat vector because malicious actors have tried to insert back doors into open-source communities, and a company may unknowingly rely on components later hit by a zero-day.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Supply-chain trust in open-source firmware/software is now a first-order chip-security risk, not just an IT-software concern — raises the case for hardware vendors auditing upstream open-source dependencies the way software companies do.
insights.locator: Petr: ...if you have any open-source software

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr frames the core defensive gap as visibility: without knowing what software and hardware components are actually in a deployed system, a company cannot even determine whether a newly disclosed zero-day vulnerability affects it, let alone fix or defend against it.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Component-inventory/visibility tooling is a prerequisite market opportunity ahead of any patch/defense tooling — a two-stage security-tooling buildout (visibility first, remediation second) that investors can use to sequence which vendors benefit first.
insights.quote: Let’s say we find a new zero-day vulnerability. Do you know if your system is impacted? How do you know?
insights.locator: Petr: ...So every layer now needs a defense system

themes.theme: CRA and regulation as the real forcing function

insights.claim: Arteris' Michal Siwinski states the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) deadline that 'has teeth' for semiconductors is September 11, 2026.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A hard, dated regulatory deadline (Sept 11, 2026) is a near-term catalyst for semiconductor security-compliance spend across any company selling into the EU — a concrete date to monitor for compliance-driven order flow at security IP vendors.
insights.quote: For semiconductors, the one that has teeth is September 11 of this year.
insights.locator: Siwinski: For semiconductors, the one that has teeth

insights.claim: Synaptics' Mohit Arora notes CRA penalties are steep — around 4% of annual revenue — meaning the largest companies face the greatest absolute financial liability for non-compliance.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A revenue-scaled penalty structure means large-cap semiconductor and OEM names have the strongest balance-sheet incentive to fund security compliance quickly — a differentiator when assessing which customers will prioritize security IP spend first.
insights.quote: the penalties are pretty hefty — like 4% of your annual revenue. So the bigger the company, the greater the liability.
insights.locator: Arora: Just to add, the penalties are pretty hefty

insights.claim: As of this discussion, no company has yet been fined under the CRA, and panelists (Petr, Giles) are uncertain whether the regulation has changed actual security behavior versus merely raising awareness — with Giles citing a pattern where regulatory deadlines get repeatedly paused once implementation costs become apparent, as happened with the U.S. Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) after a change in government.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A credible risk exists that CRA enforcement slips the way SSDF did, which would blunt the expected compliance-driven security-spend catalyst — investors should track actual fines/enforcement post-Sept 2026, not just the deadline passing, before pricing in a compliance spending wave.
insights.quote: No one has gotten fined yet.
insights.locator: Petr: No one has gotten fined yet.

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel says CRA has already produced one concrete behavioral change: companies he 'thought would never change' are now putting a much larger root of trust on-chip than any vendor at the table had built alone, with some bending toward OCP-driven root-of-trust designs, largely because CRA compels vendors selling worldwide to support security for customers who previously would not pay for it.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that CRA is already driving root-of-trust silicon adoption — a bullish, near-term (not speculative) demand signal for root-of-trust IP suppliers (Synopsys, Rambus, Arteris) tied to OCP standardization.
insights.quote: Companies I thought would never say yes are saying yes.
insights.locator: Hinkel: CRA has been a very positive change

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel argues security investment scales with the value of the service being protected, using Apple's iPhone as the case study: Apple's per-device security investment has grown from a few dollars to hundreds of dollars over time, which lets it sustain a retail price two to three times competitors' because customers trust it with high-value services (PINs, passwords, personal data).
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Frames security spend as a margin- and price-premium enabler, not just a cost center — a template for evaluating which device/services companies (beyond Apple) can convert security investment into pricing power via monetized high-value services.
insights.locator: Hinkel: ...If you look at the iPhone over time

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel says product managers who want to sell high-value subscription services on a device must be told explicitly that doing so requires a service-level agreement and materially more security spend than a device that 'just does the basics,' because failure exposes them to government fines in Europe or lawsuits in the U.S.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Ties security capex directly to services-revenue strategy — any company pivoting hardware toward recurring high-value services (health data, payments, biometrics) should be modeled as needing a step-change in security spend, with legal/regulatory downside if it skips this.
insights.locator: Hinkel: I’ve had a lot of discussions about the positive

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr notes the U.S. military and its prime contractors (Boeing, Airbus, and their suppliers) are a persistent, independent driver of security investment, continually pressuring suppliers on security regardless of commercial market incentives.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Defense-linked demand is a more reliable, less cyclical driver of security IP revenue than consumer-market pull — relevant for assessing revenue durability at security IP suppliers with defense-adjacent customers.
insights.locator: Petr: The U.S. military also drives a lot

themes.theme: Post-quantum cryptography transition and the PKA bottleneck

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel clarifies that the U.S. government's executive order on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness did not actually move up the underlying deadlines: full deprecation of vulnerable algorithms is still about five years out, but algorithms must be available on products within three years — the confusion came from how the order was communicated, not a real acceleration.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Investors tracking PQC-driven chip/IP demand should anchor to the 3-year product-availability date, not headlines about accelerated urgency, when modeling the timing of PQC silicon revenue.
insights.locator: Hinkel: The way I viewed the executive order

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel identifies the Public Key Accelerator (PKA) industry — not chip hardware or firmware broadly — as the long pole in PQC readiness, describing existing PKA designs as 'ancient technology,' a 'patchwork' built through successive patches that was never architected to be reconfigurable or upgradable at scale for new/hybrid algorithms.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Identifies PKA redesign as the critical-path bottleneck for the entire PQC transition — a specific, investable sub-segment (crypto-accelerator IP vendors like Synopsys, Rambus) that must be rebuilt before PQC mandates can actually be met industry-wide.
insights.quote: It’s a patch upon patches. It’s a spaghetti work of stuff. It was never organized to be deployable and changeable at scale.
insights.locator: Hinkel: ...The problem that came up at a PQC conference
